translations.title: As After a Dream...
translations.text:
As after a dream,
I could not say
at what instant it happened.
They were calling.
Something already begun could not wait.

I felt strange at first,
I admit it—so many years
that passed as though on the moon...
I cannot now say exactly
what I sought, what my hope was,
because at a certain instant
everything wavered: they were calling.
And I felt close.
A little fresh air,
something as natural as a sound,
grows if one suddenly listens.

But from now on it will always be the same.
For suddenly time is full
to overflowing. Each morning
brings, as Auden says, irregular verbs
that must be learned, or painful decisions
awaiting judgment.
Still,
there are people who count on me. My friends,
or better, my companions, need,
want the same thing I want,
and love me too, just
as I love myself.

So I can scarcely remember
what became of several years of my life,
or where I was going when I woke
and found I was not alone.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Nothing Is as Sweet as a Room...
translations.text:
Nothing is as sweet as a room
for two, when we no longer love each other too much,
outside the city, in a quiet hotel,
with doubtful couples and some child with swollen glands,

except this slight sense
of unreality. Something like summer
at my parents' house long ago,
like train journeys at night. I call you

to say nothing you do not
already know, or perhaps
to kiss vaguely
the same lips.

You have left the balcony.
The room has grown dark
while we look at each other tenderly,
uncomfortable at not feeling the weight of three years.

Everything is the same; it seems
yesterday did not happen. And this nostalgic taste
that silences leave in the mouth
may lead us to mistake

our feelings. But not
without some reserve, for underneath
something pulls harder and it is (to put it
perhaps a little less inaccurately)
difficult to remember that we love each other,
except with a certain vagueness, and Saturday,
which is today, lies so close
to late yesterday and to the day after

tomorrow
morning...
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: When I Was Younger...
translations.text:
When I was younger
(well, actually, it would be better to say
very young),
some years before
we met and
newly arrived in the city,
I often thought about life.
My family
was quite rich, and I was a student.

My childhood was memories of a house
with a schoolroom, pantry, and wardrobe key,
of a time when well-to-do
families,
as their name suggests,
spent endless summers
at Villa Estefanía or La Torre
del Mirador,
and beyond lay the rest of the world
with gravel paths and rustic
summerhouses, decorated with showy hydrangeas,
all a little selfish and past its time.
I was born (forgive me)
in the age of pergolas and tennis.

Life, however, had strange limits
and, stranger still, a certain tendency
to draw back.
People told painful stories,
inexplicable things that had happened
no one knew where, sad faces,
cellars cold as temples.
Something muffled
endured in the distance,
and it was possible, they said at home,
to go blind from a shiver.

From my small fortunate kingdom
I kept this habit of warmth
and an impossible leaning toward myth.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: In the Name of Today
translations.text:
In the name of today, the twenty-sixth
of April, nineteen hundred
and fifty-nine, a Sunday
of clouds and sun, at three
—as time pronounces it—
in the afternoon, when I begin
this exercise in the first person
singular, indicative,

and likewise in the name of the bird
and the foam of the almond tree,
of the world, in short, that we inhabit,
I will tell you what I understand.
But before going further,
from this page I want
to send greetings to my parents,
who will not be reading me.

For you, whom I do not name,
my love—and now I speak seriously—
for you, sun of my days
and nights, marvelous
great prize of my life,
of my whole life, what can I
say, what would you have me write
at the threshold of these verses?

Finally, to my friends,
fellow travelers,
and above all to you,
Carlos, Ángel,
Alfonso and Pepe, Gabriel
and Gabriel, Pepe (Caballero),
and to my nephew Miguel,
Joseagustín and Blas de Otero,

to you sinners
like me, ashamed
of the blows I have not received,
gentlemen by birth
and writers of social poetry
out of bad conscience,
I dedicate a remembrance too,
and to the public in general.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Friendship over Time
translations.text:
The days pass slowly,
and often we were alone.
But then there are happy moments
to let ourselves be in friendship.

Look:
it is us.

A fate skillfully guided
the hours, and companionship arose.
Nights came. In their warmth
we lit up words,
words we later left behind
to rise higher:
we began to be companions
who know one another
beyond voice or gesture.
Now, yes. The gracious words
—those that no longer say things—
may rise, float lightly on the air;
for we are tangled together
in the world, vine-like
with accumulated history,
and the companionship we have formed is full,
leafy with presences.
Behind each one
his house keeps watch, the fields, the distance.

But be quiet.
I want to tell you something.
I only want to tell you we are all together.
Sometimes, while speaking, someone forgets
his arm upon mine,
and though I am silent I give thanks,
for there is peace in our bodies and among us.
I want to tell you how we brought
our lives here to recount them.
At length, with one another,
we have talked in the corner for so many months
that we know each other well, and in memory
joy is equal to sorrow.
For us pain is tender.

Ah, time! Now everything is understood.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Outskirts (VII)
translations.text:
Look at the adolescent's night.
Behind lie the demands
of day, its family of fears,

and distance passes down an avenue
of memories or graves without a city,
confused outskirts slowly

fading. The night takes hold
—right up to the heavens each time; close by,
the temple beats at the center.

Beneath a thick rustle absence
spreads and returns toward eyes
open without sleep, sensitive. Something

that must be a breeze, like a trace
of coolness fading, breathes out
from the balcony through which night entered.

Its stealthy fingers of darkness
brush the exasperated skin, seek
the withdrawn tips of the eyelids.

And night comes up to the eyes,
questions the motionless pupils,
strikes what is most tender and still resists

at the instant of yielding, bursts
into the body, night, spilling out,
and runs, waking held-back

hollows, substances, dry channels,
like a torrent of mercury,
and dissipates as it courses through the body.

It is itself a body, flesh, an eyelid
thinned to pain, the beating
of so much sleepless death,

the palpable form of absence—blind
with absorbed night, thought turns.
And the arsenic-red rose, there

where memory was, rises,
a head of currents toward the complete
sleep on the other side of night.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: From Here to Eternity
translations.text:
First, without doubt, comes this widening
of the breath, almost anguishing,
and the peculiar resonance of the air,
like a great bell in the void,
bringing me the scents
of rockrose from the mountains,
more fragrant for their distance,
and of so many summers together
in my childhood.

Then there is the preliminary
roundabout, with its modest attempt at a garden,
a world abbreviated, renewed, and pure
without too much conviction, and at its far end
the predictable statue and the entrance portico
to the magnificent avenue,
to the famous capital.

And life, taking on
a panoramic character,
the immensity of an instant, almost anguishing too
—like dawn at a campsite
or the entrance to a nativity scene—life spreads out
again beneath the rarefied sky
as we accelerate.

For there is always something more, something spectral,
as though invisibly taken away,
and yet real.
I think of livid districts, streets
or lost roads leading to villages
in the distance, like those in a nativity scene,
and I see again corners of battered brick
and lonely level crossings, and faces
leaning out to watch us, tiny figures
left behind forever, in memory
like road workers.

And perhaps that is all. Around us
facades loom, and people stand on the pavement
at the first traffic light.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Definitely...
translations.text:
Definitely
it seems confirmed that the coming
winter will be hard.

The rains came early, and the Government,
meeting in its council of ministers,
may at this hour be studying
unemployment relief
or the right to dismiss workers,
or perhaps, isolated in an ocean,
it simply waits for the storm to pass
and for the day to come, the day when at last
things cease to go wrong.

On this October night,
reading between the lines of the newspaper,
I have stopped to hear the heartbeat
of silence in my room, the neighbors'
conversations as they go to bed,
all those sounds
that suddenly recover a life
and a meaning of their own, mysterious.

And I have thought of the thousands of human beings,
men and women who at this very moment,
with the first shiver,
have begun again to ask about their worries,
the weariness they already anticipate,
their anxiety about this winter,

while outside it rains.
All along the Catalan coast it rains
with real cruelty, with smoke and low clouds,
blackening walls,
dripping from factories, seeping
into poorly lit workshops.
And the water carries toward the sea seeds
just beginning to grow, mixed with mud,
trees, odd shoes, abandoned tools,
everything tumbled together
with the first protested bills of exchange.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Dawn Song
translations.text:
Wake up. The bed is colder
and the dirty sheets lie on the floor.
Through the gallery's transoms
morning comes,
colored like a coat for the changing season
and a woman's garter.

Wake up, dimly thinking
that the night porter has called you.
And listen in the silence: one after another
in the distance, the trams carrying people to work
can be heard growing hoarse.
It is dawn.

Cut flowers will pile up
at the stalls on the Ramblas,
and the birds—the bastards—will whistle
from the plane trees as they watch the dark mass
of humanity return to bed
after dawn.

Remember the room where you slept.
Bury your head in the pillows,
still feeling the irritation and cold
that dawn brings
beside the body we liked so much
last night,

and think that you ought to get up.
Think of the still-dark house
where you will go to change your clothes,
and the office, where you must fight off sleep,
and the many other things that announce themselves
at dawn.

Though beside you you hear the murmur
of someone else's breathing. Though you seek
a little warmth between half-asleep thighs
that begin to tremble. Though love
remains sweet
after dawn.

Beside the body I liked so much
naked last night, let me turn on
the light so we can kiss face to face
at dawn.
For I know the day that waits for me,
and not for pleasure.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Anniversary Song
translations.text:
Because it has already been six years since then,
because there is still nothing on earth
as sweet as a room for two,
if it is yours and mine;
because even time, that poor relation
who has seen better days,
seems today to favor happiness,
let us sing, joyfully!

And then let us get up later,
as on a Sunday. Let the full morning
pass as we make love again,
but better: in a way
the night could not imagine,
while the room fills
with sun and peaceful neighbors, like time,
and tranquil history.

The echo of days of pleasure,
desire, music in tune
within the heart, which I have scarcely put
in my poems, for fear of seeming romantic;
all the perfume, all the unfaithful past,
what was sweet and now brings longing:
do you not see how it sinks into the reality
that you and I once dreamed of?

Reality—not too beautiful—
with the difficulties of being two,
its shameful nights of love without desire
and desire without love,
which six centuries of sleeping alone
would not repay. And with
its vague transitions from betrayal to boredom,
from boredom to betrayal.

Life is not a dream; you know
we tend to forget that.
But a little dreaming, no more, just a touch
this once, leaving
the rest of the story unspoken, and for an instant
—while you and I wish each other
a happy, long life together—I am sure
it can do no harm.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.
